title: Employment transitions depend not only on jobs but on the public-service systems that match, train, protect, and reach people through shocks
source_unit: Inter-American Development Bank, OECD, and World Association of Public Employment Services, The World of Public Employment Services 2026: Delivering in a Changing World of Work
geography: Public employment services across global country systems, with 78 service profiles from 74 countries and comparative policy information

denominator.unit: public employment service profiles from 74 countries represented in the publication

comparative_scope.value: the publication updates structured and comparable information on the organization, structure, and practices of public employment services worldwide

institutional_variation.value: public employment services vary in institutional and policy arrangements, delivery structures, and operating practices

policy_endpoint.value: comparative service evidence is intended to inform future labor-market policy components

observations.method: Global survey, structured comparative data, policy information, and country profiles compiled by IDB, OECD, and WAPES.
observations.uncertainty: Country and service profiles are not a common causal evaluation; institutional labels and reported practices may not be fully comparable or predictive of individual service outcomes.
observations.subgroup: Jobseekers, workers at risk of displacement, employers, public employment-service staff, migrants, and people facing the greatest difficulty finding work.
observations.counterinterpretation: Different institutional models can work under different labor-market and administrative conditions; variation does not by itself mean one system is ineffective.

observations.period: 2026; digital maturity and shock response in public employment services

denominator.unit: comparative public-employment-service digital and resilience framework

digital_maturity.value: the publication presents data and analysis on the digital maturity of public employment services

shock_response.value: public employment services are examined for how they respond to shocks and strengthen labor-market resilience

delivery_tradeoff.value: digital systems can expand reach and coordination but require attention to access, capability, and institutional design

observations.method: Comparative IDB/OECD/WAPES survey and policy analysis of service organization, digital maturity, and responses to labor-market shocks.
observations.uncertainty: Digital maturity is not equivalent to service quality, successful placement, accessibility, or fair treatment; the report does not establish one universal digital model.
observations.subgroup: People with limited connectivity or digital skills, displaced workers, migrants, employers, frontline staff, and communities experiencing labor-market shocks.
observations.counterinterpretation: Blended and human-supported delivery may be more effective than maximal automation where trust, language, disability access, or complex needs matter.

observations.period: 2026; employment transitions for migrants and people facing severe access barriers

migrant_support.value: the publication considers how public employment services support employment transitions for migrants

hardest_to_place.value: partnerships with the social economy are examined as a route to support people facing the greatest difficulty finding work

transition_bundle.value: matching, skills, information, social-economy partnership, and service access operate as a transition bundle rather than a single placement event

observations.method: IDB/OECD/WAPES comparative analysis of public employment-service transition support, target groups, and partnerships.
observations.uncertainty: The report does not show that every listed service reaches migrants or hard-to-place people equally, nor that participation produces stable employment or income security.
observations.subgroup: Migrants, long-term unemployed people, workers with disabilities or care constraints, young entrants, social-economy organizations, and employers.
observations.counterinterpretation: Targeted services can stigmatize or segment users if they are poorly designed; universal access with tailored support may sometimes be preferable.

denominator.unit: public employment policy and institutional design synthesis frame

service_role.value: public employment services connect jobseekers, workers at risk, employers, training, and labor-market policy

resilience_route.value: service capacity can support transitions and labor-market resilience when aligned with shocks, local conditions, and target-group needs

governance_question.value: the key design question is how public systems combine digital tools, human support, partnerships, and accountability

observations.method: Comparative report synthesis across public employment-service organization, practices, digital systems, partnerships, and shock response.
observations.uncertainty: This is an institutional mechanism route, not a causal estimate of resilience or a claim that public employment services determine labor-market outcomes alone.
observations.subgroup: Jobseekers, employers, service workers, local administrations, national labor ministries, training providers, and social-economy partners.
observations.counterinterpretation: Macroeconomic demand, housing, transport, care, wage levels, and employer practices may constrain outcomes even when employment services are well designed.

related_sources.claim: OECD Employment Outlook 2026 provides complementary regional labor-market and transition context.
OECD employment policy page links public employment-service modernization and related work.

boundary: This record adds a public-employment-service route across institutional variation, digital maturity, shock response, migrant transitions, social-economy partnerships, and labor-market resilience. It uses comparative survey and policy information, not respondent-level job-search histories, individual placement records, case-management files, causal service evaluations, or proof that digitization improves outcomes for every group.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official IDB/OECD/WAPES publication page reviewed for global survey scope, 78 service profiles from 74 countries, institutional variation, digital maturity, shock response, migrant support, social-economy partnerships, and policy framing.
